p: Maria was on Highway 34 by 7:10, driving toward the hospital where she'd spent fourteen years of nights.

Greeley looked the same from the parking lot. Brick, a newer glass wing, the helipad, the smokers' bench that had been moved three times and still drew smokers. What was different was the lobby. Four people in business clothes stood by the information desk with laptops and lanyards, and the hospital president was shaking their hands with the smile of a man who had been told about them twenty minutes ago.

The Joint Commission doesn't call ahead. That's the point. Surveyors show up, ask for the census, pick patients, and follow their care through the building to see whether the hospital does what its policies say. They talk to nurses. They open cabinets. They ask a tech on the night shift where the fire extinguisher is and watch where the tech's eyes go.
Her phone buzzed while she was still in the car. Marcus. laramie queue still clean. digging into why nobody got paged. don't have it yet.
Then Kiran. When the backlog posted, the Laramie house sup texted the critical values to the nurses' cell phones. Just so you know before somebody else tells you.
Then Ochoa, who was apparently already at his desk. Greeley's yours for the week. Every tracer touches something you own. Don't hide anything and don't perform. Breakfast tomorrow, the diner, 6:30.

Maria sat in the car a minute longer. Three hours of lab results that nobody saw. Four surveyors who would spend the week looking for exactly that kind of gap. She had owned all of it for about a month.
She clipped on her badge and went in through the employee entrance, the way she always had.
The first tracer went to the ICU. Of course it did. Maria followed the surveyor, a nurse from Ohio with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair, through doors she could have opened in her sleep.

Bev Hart was charge nurse. Bev had precepted Maria on her first night shift eighteen years ago and still called her "kid." The surveyor asked Bev a simple question. Your EHR goes down right now. How does a critical lab result reach you?
Bev opened her mouth and nothing came. Her eyes went to the shelf where the 2019 downtime binder used to be. It wasn't there. Then they went to Maria.

Bev says she'd call the lab and the lab would call her. That's half right. Afterward Maria tells the surveyor that the unit's downtime binder is missing, that her team owns the downtime procedures, and that a recent outage at another hospital showed the same gap. The surveyor writes for a long time. Bev squeezes Maria's arm in the hallway. You always did tell on yourself, kid.

At noon Maria took a call in a supply closet. The Laramie quality director wanted to know who was leading the review of last night. Three hours of delayed lab results, one critical potassium, no harm that anyone knew of yet.
I can write it up, Marcus said on the same call. It's my interface. Kiran offered to pull the list of every affected result. Everyone was helpful. Nobody was sure whose job it was.

She files the report from the closet. The patient safety officer takes the lead by two o'clock and names a team: the Laramie lab, nursing, the house supervisor, Marcus for the technical cause, and Maria for the systems side. The review asks two questions: why it broke and why nobody knew. Marcus gets the first one.
The Laramie house supervisor called back that afternoon. She sounded like she'd been up all night, because she had.
I texted the criticals to the nurses' personal phones. Name, room, value. I know. I'd do it again. It was faster than walking six units.
She wasn't wrong that it was faster. She also wasn't wrong that it put patient names on a dozen personal phones. Cascade's policy didn't say anything about downtime messaging at all.

Joan Whitfield, the privacy officer, and Nate Ostrowski, the CISO, meet her Thursday. The draft names the hospital's secure messaging app on unit phones as the only channel for PHI, keeps the phone callback for critical results, and spells out who verifies the values once the system is back. The house supervisor reads it and says, Okay. That I can do at 2 AM.
At 8 PM the Greeley nurse manager for the medical floors caught Maria in the parking garage. Doug had a box of new downtime binders under one arm and a sheet of green stickers in his hand.
Printed twenty of these. I'll put one on every unit tonight. The stickers say reviewed. I figured I'd date them last spring, so it doesn't look like we scrambled.
He looked exhausted and proud of himself. He'd had a long day too.

Doug winces, then laughs. Yeah. Okay. That was dumb. They put the binders out together, dated today. When a surveyor asks the next morning, the nurse says they came out last night, and she read hers. The surveyor nods.

Day two, the emergency department. The surveyor asked to see how the ED registers patients when Corvane is down. A registrar pulled the paper downtime form and walked through it with a made-up patient, a teenager with a broken wrist.
The paper form had been copied years ago from a registration screen two systems back. Insurance carrier and policy number were the first two boxes. The triage section was on the back.
The registrar did exactly what the form said and asked the pretend teenager about insurance first. The surveyor wrote it down.

She has a registration analyst pull the electronic quick registration build, and it has the same order. Both get fixed within the week with the ED director and compliance at the table: name, birth date, complaint, triage. Insurance after the medical screening exam starts.
Aisha Rahman found Maria in the cafeteria at lunch, between tracers. Aisha was the CMIO, a hospitalist who moved fast and thought in data.

Quick favor. My fellow needs a de-identified extract for a sepsis study. All septic admissions, last two years, all eleven hospitals. No names, no MRNs. Just admit date, discharge date, ZIP code, age, labs, outcome. Can Kiran run it this week?
Maria looked at the list on the napkin. Admit dates. ZIP codes.

Aisha frowns, then nods. Fine. You're right, the dates are the whole study. Maria sends it to Joan Whitfield, the privacy officer, who sets up a data use agreement and checks the research approval. The fellow gets the extract in two weeks, legally.
Marcus called that evening with what sounded like good news. The regional HIE had noticed Laramie's feed went quiet during the outage, and while they were at it, they'd asked a question.

They want to move Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins under Cascade's HIE agreement. Right now those three still send through the old MedaLink arrangement. I can repoint the feeds Friday. One problem. Rawlins has the behavioral health clinic, and its substance use treatment program. And MedaLink kept its own opt out list. I don't know what Cascade's agreement does with either.
It was a technical question on the surface. Maria knew it wasn't.

Maria calls Joan Whitfield that night. Joan answers on the second ring and asks three questions Maria hadn't thought of. The plan they agree on carries the MedaLink opt out list into the new agreement, keeps the clinic's Part 2 records out unless a patient consents, and moves the feeds two weeks later than Marcus wanted.
Day three. The Greeley medical staff president caught Maria after a meeting with a printed request signed by twenty-two physicians.
Patients see their lab results in the portal before we do. They panic and call at night. We want a seventy-two hour hold on every result before it releases. Your team can build that, right?
Her team could build it in an afternoon. That was the problem.

Maria brings compliance and Joan into the room. Results release on time unless a law says otherwise. A physician can hold one specific patient's result after documenting that seeing it could endanger that patient's life or physical safety. Worry about a result isn't enough. Patients can choose to wait for a call. Kiran adds a portal note that says the doctor will follow up. The medical staff president isn't thrilled, but he signs it.
That afternoon a text arrived from a number Maria hadn't saved yet.
A text from Joan Whitfield. Joan again. Thanks for the HIE call. Anything else from Laramie I should know about?

The spreadsheet was Kiran's list of every delayed Laramie result, with names, record numbers, and values. A Laramie lab analyst had emailed it to a personal account to work on at home. The analyst had told Kiran, and Kiran had told Maria, and Maria hadn't told anyone yet.

Joan listens without interrupting, then asks for the account type, the time, and whether the analyst forwarded it. The assessment takes two days. Joan handles the analyst with care. When it's done, Joan says, You called me before I had to call you. Keep doing that.
By Thursday Maria had a draft plan to fix downtime procedures across Cascade. One binder template, one set of steps, one drill schedule, for every site.
Kiran read it and tapped one line. Home health nurses are in people's living rooms. They don't have a unit, or a binder shelf, or a lab down the hall. And the clinics close at five.

Home health gets offline visit notes on a tablet and a call tree. The clinics get a schedule printout at close of day. Rawlins, a critical access hospital with one IT tech, gets a simpler version Cheyenne will back up. It's four plans that share one spine.
Thursday night Maria drafted an email to every clinical manager: from now on, all downtime procedures follow the attached steps. It felt good to write. She had her finger over Send.
Then she thought about the 2019 binder nobody could find, and the fact that nobody could tell her who had approved it.

She files it with the policy committee. The procedure gets a named owner, an approval path through nursing and IT, a version number, a review date a year out, and a training plan. The old 2019 version is formally retired so nobody finds it again.
Friday morning, the last day of the survey, a woman stopped Maria at the ICU desk. Her mother had been discharged to a rehab center in Loveland, and the rehab doctor wanted the records.

I'm her health care power of attorney. I have the paper. Medical records told me they can only print it, it's twenty-five cents a page, and it's eleven hundred pages. Can't you just put it on a flash drive?
She looked about forty. She had the same tired eyes Maria saw in the mirror after night shift. For a second Maria thought of Lucia, someday, standing at a desk like this one.

Maria walks her to medical records, checks the power of attorney with the HIM manager, and asks why it has to be paper. There's no good reason. The daughter leaves with an encrypted electronic copy that afternoon. The HIM manager adds a note to fix the default.

The exit conference was at three o'clock on Friday in the Greeley board room. Four surveyors at one end of the table, the hospital's leaders at the other, Ochoa in a chair along the wall like furniture, which was what he'd promised.
The lead surveyor read the summary in a flat, kind voice. Medication management, no findings. Infection control, no findings. Patient rights, no findings. Then she turned a page.

Preliminary finding: downtime procedures. The hospital does not consistently ensure that staff can carry out downtime procedures for its information systems. Downtime materials were missing or outdated on two units, and staff interviewed could not describe how critical results would reach them during an outage.
One finding. The hospital would stay accredited. And the one thing the surveyors had written up was the thing Maria owned.
Joan Whitfield, across the table, caught her eye and gave a small nod. It might have meant sorry. It might have meant good. With Joan, she was learning, it could mean both.

In the parking lot Ochoa walked her to her car. You told them before they found it, he said. They noticed. Now go find out why your hospitals didn't know their own procedures. Then fix that, not the binders.
Lucia was at the kitchen table when she got home, laptop open, a nursing school essay prompt on the screen. Describe a time a rule protected a patient. She'd written two sentences and deleted them.
Do you have one? she asked. A rule that actually saved somebody?

Maria thought about Bev's empty shelf, a pretend teenager with a broken wrist stuck behind an insurance question, a list of patients who'd said no to sharing. Most of the rules I know about, she said, sitting down, somebody got hurt first. That's how they got written.
Lucia looked at her for a long moment. That's kind of a sad essay, Mom. But she started typing.

It had been a hard week that went well. Maria had told the truth to a surveyor on her old unit and tried to put every problem in front of the person who owned it. None of that changed the finding. The finding was about the work before her, and now it was hers.
At 10:15 PM her phone lit up on the counter. Marcus. found why nobody noticed laramie. it's not the interface. you'll want to sit down for this one. tues?
